<reason>A narrowly wins by distinguishing scheduling authority from immunity to binding drought constraints. B’s finite neutral-determination proposal successfully answered the Egyptian-veto objection, making this close. However, B insufficiently explained why prospective flow commitments and independent scrutiny required prior authorization of every timetable, repeatedly treating A’s preventive safeguards as merely post-harm remedies. A also exposed the weakness in treating electricity-related losses as recoverable simply because Ethiopia’s deprivation already exists.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A’s strongest rebuttal challenged B’s prevention-versus-compensation framing: binding flow-based duties could constrain retention before shortages while leaving Ethiopia scheduling authority. B answered with “self-grading,” but did not squarely establish why those constraints necessarily depended on an external order approving the timetable.</best_rebuttal>
